questions.enonce_markdown: The real valued function $f$ is defined as $f: x \mapsto \dfrac{4x}{x-1}$, $x \in \mathbb{R}$, $x \neq 1$. Show that $f$ is injective. (4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
A function is injective (one-to-one) if $f(x_1) = f(x_2)$ implies $x_1 = x_2$ for all $x_1, x_2$ in the domain.

Let $x_1, x_2 \in \mathbb{R} \setminus \{1\}$ with $f(x_1) = f(x_2)$:

$$\frac{4x_1}{x_1 - 1} = \frac{4x_2}{x_2 - 1}.$$

Cross-multiplying (both denominators are non-zero):

$$4x_1(x_2 - 1) = 4x_2(x_1 - 1) \;\Longrightarrow\; x_1x_2 - x_1 = x_1x_2 - x_2 \;\Longrightarrow\; x_1 = x_2.$$

Hence $f$ is injective. $\blacksquare$

**Remark (second proof).** $f(x) = \dfrac{4(x-1) + 4}{x-1} = 4 + \dfrac{4}{x-1}$, and $f'(x) = -\dfrac{4}{(x-1)^2} < 0$ for every $x \neq 1$, so $f$ is strictly decreasing on each of $(-\infty, 1)$ and $(1, \infty)$. The value $4$ is never taken, and the values taken on $(-\infty,1)$ are all below $4$ while those taken on $(1,\infty)$ are all above $4$, so no value is taken twice.

questions.enonce_markdown: The real valued function $f$ is defined as $f: x \mapsto \dfrac{4x}{x-1}$, $x \in \mathbb{R}$, $x \neq 1$. Find $(f \circ f)(x)$, stating its domain. (3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
$(f \circ f)(x) = f(f(x))$, so replace $x$ by $f(x) = \dfrac{4x}{x-1}$ in the formula for $f$:

$$(f\circ f)(x) = \frac{4\cdot\dfrac{4x}{x-1}}{\dfrac{4x}{x-1} - 1} = \frac{\dfrac{16x}{x-1}}{\dfrac{4x - (x-1)}{x-1}} = \frac{16x}{3x+1}.$$

**Domain.** $x$ must be in the domain of the inner function, so $x \neq 1$. Also $f(x)$ must be in the domain of the outer function, so $f(x) \neq 1$:

$$\frac{4x}{x-1} = 1 \;\Longleftrightarrow\; 4x = x - 1 \;\Longleftrightarrow\; x = -\frac13,$$

so $x \neq -\dfrac13$ (this is the value that makes $3x + 1 = 0$).

$$\boxed{(f \circ f)(x) = \frac{16x}{3x+1}, \quad x \in \mathbb{R},\ x \neq 1,\ x \neq -\tfrac13}$$

Note that the point $x = 1$ must stay excluded even though the simplified formula $\dfrac{16x}{3x+1}$ is defined there (value $4$): $f(1)$ does not exist.

**Check.** $f(2) = 8$ and $f(8) = \dfrac{32}{7}$; the formula gives $\dfrac{16 \times 2}{3 \times 2 + 1} = \dfrac{32}{7}$.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Two statements $p$ and $q$ are given by:

$p$: The principal goes to the ministry,

$q$: The principal will meet the minister.

Write out the following propositions in ordinary English:

(c) $p \wedge q$,

(d) $\sim p \vee \sim q$,

(e) $\sim p \Rightarrow \sim q$. (3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
The symbols are: $\wedge$ = "and", $\vee$ = "or", $\sim$ = "not", $\Rightarrow$ = "if ... then".

(c) $p \wedge q$: **The principal goes to the ministry and the principal will meet the minister.**

(d) $\sim p \vee \sim q$: **The principal does not go to the ministry or the principal will not meet the minister.** (At least one of the two things does not happen.)

(e) $\sim p \Rightarrow \sim q$: **If the principal does not go to the ministry, then the principal will not meet the minister.**

Remark: (d) is the negation of (c) by De Morgan's law, $\sim(p \wedge q) \equiv \sim p \vee \sim q$.
